<p class="project-name">The Productive Role of Error in AI-Driven Modeling</p>

# When AI gets science wrong, what can we learn?

[A Sloan Foundation project studying how errors in AI-driven scientific models
can be productive: how failures lead to new understanding, stronger models and
earned trust. We focus on climate and Earth system science.]{.lede}

::: {.cell-actions}
[Read the question](about.qmd){.button .button-primary}
[Get involved](contact.qmd){.button .button-secondary}
:::

::: {.latest-note}
**Latest:** [Call for extended abstracts and speakers, February 2027](workshop.qmd)
· Scroll to run the notebook
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notebook-cell .code-cell tabindex="0" data-cell="2" role="group" aria-label="Cell 2"}
::: {.cell-prompt}
<span class="prompt-label" aria-hidden="true"></span><button type="button" class="run-cell" aria-label="Run cell 2"><svg viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path d="M4 2.5v11l9-5.5z"/></svg></button>
:::

::: {.code-input}
<code><span class="code-function">ask</span>(<span class="code-string">&quot;What happens when an AI model gets it wrong?&quot;</span>)</code>
:::

::: {.output-prompt aria-hidden="true"}
:::

::: {.cell-output}
It happens all the time. AI models in science produce biased results, fail on
data unlike what they were trained on, break known physical laws, and crash in
ways their developers didn't expect.

The usual response is to fix the error and move on. But when scientists dig
into an error, they often learn something they couldn't have learned
otherwise.
:::
:::

::: {.notebook-cell .code-cell tabindex="0" data-cell="3" role="group" aria-label="Cell 3"}
::: {.cell-prompt}
<span class="prompt-label" aria-hidden="true"></span><button type="button" class="run-cell" aria-label="Run cell 3"><svg viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path d="M4 2.5v11l9-5.5z"/></svg></button>
:::

::: {.code-input}
<code><span class="code-function">forecast</span>(<span class="code-variable">ai_weather_model</span>, <span class="code-variable">days</span><span class="code-operator">=</span><span class="code-number">14</span>)</code>
:::

<!-- Cells 3–4 follow the case in the proposal (Bonev et al. 2023;
O'Loughlin et al. 2025). Ryan: confirm the wording before launch. -->

::: {.cell-output .error-output}
[InstabilityError]{.error-name}: forecast became unstable after about 10 days

An AI model trained to emulate weather prediction, a Fourier neural operator,
gave good short-range forecasts. Then, about ten days in, its forecasts broke
down.
:::
:::

::: {.notebook-cell .code-cell tabindex="0" data-cell="4" role="group" aria-label="Cell 4"}
::: {.cell-prompt}
<span class="prompt-label" aria-hidden="true"></span><button type="button" class="run-cell" aria-label="Run cell 4"><svg viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path d="M4 2.5v11l9-5.5z"/></svg></button>
:::

::: {.code-input}
<code><span class="code-function">diagnose</span>(<span class="code-variable">error</span>)</code>
:::

::: {.output-prompt aria-hidden="true"}
:::

::: {.cell-output}
Instead of abandoning the model, researchers traced the failure to one design
choice. The model's math assumed a flat map that repeats at its edges, not a
round Earth. Rebuilt with transforms made for a sphere (spherical harmonics),
it ran stably for a full simulated year.

> The error pointed to what the model was missing: the shape of the planet.

::: {.cell-source}
Sources: [Bonev et al. 2023](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/bonev23a.html),
*Spherical Fourier Neural Operators*, ICML;
[O'Loughlin et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-18-787-2025),
*Geoscientific Model Development*.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notebook-cell .code-cell tabindex="0" data-cell="5" role="group" aria-label="Cell 5"}
::: {.cell-prompt}
<span class="prompt-label" aria-hidden="true"></span><button type="button" class="run-cell" aria-label="Run cell 5"><svg viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path d="M4 2.5v11l9-5.5z"/></svg></button>
:::

::: {.code-input}
<code><span class="code-comment"># Scientists often prefer &quot;bias&quot; or &quot;limitation&quot; to &quot;error&quot;</span><br><span class="code-function">learn_from</span>(<span class="code-variable">error</span>)</code>
:::

::: {.output-prompt aria-hidden="true"}
:::

::: {.cell-output}
Errors like this can give science three things:

- **Understanding:** working out why a model failed can show which part of it
  is responsible, a deeper kind of understanding than most explainability
  tools give.
- **Antifragility:** some systems gain from shocks rather than just surviving
  them. Models and modeling teams can come out of a failure stronger, not just
  repaired.
- **Credibility:** how errors are recorded, shared and fixed shapes whether the
  science can be trusted.

**When do errors make AI-driven science better than immediate success would
have?**

::: {.cell-source}
Sources: [O'Loughlin 2023](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13194-023-00522-z) and
[O'Loughlin et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-18-787-2025) on
understanding; Taleb 2012, *Antifragile*, on antifragility;
[Mayernik 2021](https://doi.org/10.17351/ests2021.769) on credibility.
:::
:::
:::

reading the reports, code repositories and data records where errors get
written down.
